Asymptotic Notation and Growth Comparison

Data Structures and Algorithms · Chapter 2 · Approved English chapter · 18 fully worked problems

1. Scope, prerequisites, and four reviewed university texts

This chapter turns an operation-count function into a defensible statement about its growth. It teaches the precise quantifiers behind upper, lower, tight, and strict bounds; constructive witnesses and disproof; limits and their failure modes; a proved hierarchy of logarithms, powers, exponentials, and factorials; and safe algebra with asymptotic relations. The previous chapter fixed input size and cost model. The next chapters will derive costs from loops and solve recurrences. Those techniques are not silently assumed here. Our default domain is positive integers n tending to infinity, and functions are eventually nonnegative unless a signed variant is expressly given. Elementary algebra, logarithms, induction, and limits are prerequisites; each needed fact is restated when used.

The selected written sources were actually read in their chapter-relevant pages: MIT 6.006 Recitation 1 (PDF pp. 3 and 6), Stanford CS161 Lecture 2 (pp. 6–7), Carnegie Mellon 15-451 Lecture 2 (pp. 10–11), and Kevin Wayne's Princeton algorithm-analysis slides (pp. 3–6). MIT and Stanford supply precise eventual bounds and witness methods; CMU supplies strict notation and oscillation; Princeton supplies algebraic laws, limit proofs, and parameter warnings. They were selected from a bounded pool, documented in the source audit, rather than assumed to be the four globally best courses. The source audit is part of the development record; complete public citations are at the end of this lesson. The exercises below are newly worded; a label saying inspired by identifies a reasoning pattern, not a copied question.

2. The mathematical contract behind a complexity claim

2.1 Which function is being bounded?

Let T(x) be the number of charged primitive operations executed on an instance x. If |x|=n is the specified input-size measure, the worst-case resource function is Tworst(n)=max|x|=nT(x) when the maximum and at least one such input exist. A claim such as Tworst ∈ O(n2) concerns that function under that model and encoding. It does not say every input takes quadratic time, nor does a bound on one algorithm automatically apply to every algorithm for the problem. For an empty size class use a stated alternative, such as a supremum over inputs of size at most n. For average-case cost, first specify an input distribution. For randomized algorithms, specify whether the claim bounds worst-case time over random choices, expectation, or a high-probability event.

Asymptotics ignore a fixed initial segment of sizes. They do not declare a small-input run free or a large constant irrelevant in practice. Consider two hypothetical implementations with costs A(n)=1000n and B(n)=n2. Their symbolic growth classes are Θ(n) and Θ(n2), but B(n)<A(n) for 1<n<1000. The crossover occurs at n=1000. It is a modelling example, not a measured benchmark.

2.2 Function classes are sets

For an eventually nonnegative comparison function g, O(g) is a set of functions. Writing f∈O(g) is formally precise. The conventional notation f=O(g) is read as membership, not ordinary equality; it cannot be algebraically reversed to infer equality of functions. Throughout, choose c,c1,c2>0 and an integer threshold n0 independent of n. A constant may depend on fixed parameters such as a prescribed exponent, but not on the input size it is supposed to bound.

f ∈ O(g) ⇔ ∃c>0, n0 : ∀n≥n0, 0≤f(n)≤c g(n).
f ∈ Ω(g) ⇔ ∃c>0, n0 : ∀n≥n0, 0≤c g(n)≤f(n).
f ∈ Θ(g) ⇔ ∃c1,c2>0,n0 : ∀n≥n0, 0≤c1g(n)≤f(n)≤c2g(n).

The order of quantifiers matters: one pair of constants must work for every sufficiently large input size. “For infinitely many n” is insufficient. For example, f(n)=n2 at odd sizes and f(n)=1 at even sizes satisfies f(n)≥n for infinitely many odd sizes, yet f∉Ω(n) because at arbitrarily large even sizes 1<cn for every fixed c>0. Exchanging f and g gives f∈Ω(g) ⇔ g∈O(f) when the nonnegativity assumptions hold. Tightness means both directions: Θ(g)=O(g)∩Ω(g).

2.3 Strict relations and asymptotic equivalence

In this subsection assume the comparison function g(n)>0 for every sufficiently large n. The little-oh relation is stronger than big-oh:

f ∈ o(g) ⇔ ∀ε>0, ∃nε : ∀n≥nε, 0≤f(n)<εg(n).
f ∈ ω(g) ⇔ ∀M>0, ∃nM : ∀n≥nM, f(n)>Mg(n)≥0.

The strict inequality can be replaced by a non-strict one after changing ε or M; the quantifier over every positive constant is decisive. If g(n)>0 eventually, then f∈o(g) exactly when f(n)/g(n)→0, and f∈ω(g) exactly when the ratio tends to positive infinity. Also f∈ω(g) ⇔ g∈o(f) when both ratios are eventually defined and positive. Neither o(g) nor ω(g) includes a function in Θ(g).

Asymptotic equivalence uses a stronger symbol: f∼g means f(n)/g(n)→1, with g(n)≠0 eventually. Equivalently, |f−g|/g→0 for eventually positive g, or f=g+h with |h|∈o(g). The residual h may be negative: for example, f(n)=n−1 and g(n)=n satisfy f∼g although their difference is −1. This absolute-value formulation respects our nonnegative little-oh convention. Thus f∼g ⇒ f∈Θ(g); the converse is false: 2n∈Θ(n) while 2n∼n is false. “Not in Θ(g)” is not the same as o(g) or ω(g); oscillating or incomparable functions need neither strict relation.

For signed mathematical expressions, some texts define f∈O(g) through |f(n)|≤c|g(n)|. This is useful for error terms but is not the same convention as nonnegative runtime bounds. If a polynomial has a negative leading coefficient, it is eventually negative and cannot itself model elapsed time; first determine whether the intended object is an algebraic error or a nonnegative resource. We use the absolute-value convention only when explicitly stated.

3. Prove or refute a proposed bound

3.1 Construct a witness rather than relying on a slogan

To establish f∈O(g), exhibit constants c,n0 and verify the inequality for every n≥n0. For f(n)=3n2+17n+100 and n≥1, n≤n2 and 1≤n2, so f(n)≤120n2. The lower bound is f(n)≥3n2. Consequently f∈Θ(n2) with c1=3,c2=120,n0=1. These constants are valid, not necessarily optimal. A larger threshold can yield much smaller constants.

For an eventual upper bound, finite exceptions are harmless. For example, n2−100n is negative for some positive sizes, so the runtime convention does not apply there; for n≥101 it is nonnegative and at most n2. A lower bound also needs a threshold: if n≥200, then n2−100n≥n2/2. This yields an eventual Θ claim for the eventually nonnegative function, not a claim about a runtime that is negative on small inputs.

3.2 Negating the quantifiers is the cleanest disproof

To refute f∈O(g) with positive g, show that for every proposed c>0 and n0, some n≥n0 has f(n)>cg(n). For f(n)=n2 and g(n)=n, choose an integer n>max(c,n0). Then n2>cn. A graph of the first few values cannot replace this argument: asymptotic bounds concern an unbounded tail.

Likewise, to refute f∈Ω(g), for every proposed c,n0 find a sufficiently large n with f(n)<cg(n). To refute a Θ claim it is enough to refute either its O or its Ω half. A single exceptional input does not refute an eventual claim; infinitely many unbounded counterexamples can.

3.3 The ratio method and its exact limitations

When g(n)>0 eventually, inspect r(n)=f(n)/g(n). If r(n)→0, then f∈o(g). If r(n)→L for finite L>0, choose ε=L/2 in the limit definition to obtain L/2≤r(n)≤3L/2 eventually; hence f∈Θ(g). If r(n)→∞, then f∈ω(g). If the limit does not exist, return to eventual upper and lower envelopes. A limit is a sufficient classification shortcut, not a necessary condition for Θ.

For example, f(n)=n(2+sin n) has 1≤f(n)/n≤3 for every positive integer, so f∈Θ(n). The ratio has no limit: the integer sequence sin n does not converge. One can avoid needing that nonconvergence fact by using the explicitly alternating f(n)=n for even n and f(n)=3n for odd n; the ratio alternates exactly between 1 and 3, while the Θ witnesses remain 1,3,1. Conversely, a ratio whose liminf is zero and limsup infinite can defeat both O and Ω, as Problem 9 demonstrates.

3.4 Leading terms, cancellations, and discrete transformations

For a nonzero real polynomial p(n)=adnd+⋯+a0 with positive leading coefficient ad, divide by nd: the ratio tends to ad>0, so p∈Θ(nd). If leading terms cancel, simplify the whole expression before reading a degree: (n2+n)−(n2−5n)=6n, not Θ(n2). Do not apply the “largest term wins” rule to a difference of nonnegative terms without controlling cancellation.

For n≥2, n/2≤⌊n/2⌋≤n/2 is false for odd n; a correct robust pair is n/4≤⌊n/2⌋≤n/2. Thus ⌊n/2⌋∈Θ(n). More sharply, ⌊n/2⌋=(n/2)+O(1) using the signed-error convention. Shifts by a fixed constant usually preserve polynomial and logarithmic Θ classes, but not asymptotic equivalence for every family: 2n+1=2·2n is Θ-equivalent to 2n, while their ratio is 2, not 1.

4. Growth classes, with proofs and conditions

4.1 Logarithms and changes of base

For fixed bases a,b>1, the change-of-base identity is logan=(logbn)/(logba). The denominator is a positive constant, hence logan∈Θ(logbn). This does not license discarding a logarithm whose base depends on n: lognn=1 for n>1, whereas log2n grows without bound. Also distinguish log(nk)=k log n from (log n)k, which is generally a different class. We write ln for the natural logarithm and use base 2 when a numerical binary size is intended.

For fixed k>0 and ε>0, (ln n)k∈o(nε). Put t=ln n, so the ratio becomes tke−εt. Choose an integer m>k. The exponential series gives eεt≥(εt)m/m! for t>0. Therefore

0 ≤ tk/eεt ≤ (m!/εm)tk−m → 0.

This proof covers every fixed real k>0, since m can be a larger integer. It also implies log log n∈o(log n) by applying the same fact to t=log n and a positive fractional exponent. The statement is about a fixed k; if k=k(n) increases with input size, redo the analysis.

4.2 Powers and exponentials

For real constants a<b and positive n, na/nb=na−b→0. For fixed bases 1<A<B, An/Bn=(A/B)n→0. More generally, for fixed real a and B>1, na∈o(Bn). If a>0, write Bn=en ln B and reuse the exponential-versus-power argument with t=n; for a≤0 it is immediate from na≤1 for n≥1.

A fixed multiplicative factor outside an exponential disappears inside Θ: 7·2n∈Θ(2n). A change in its exponent's coefficient generally does not: 22n=4n∉Θ(2n), since the ratio is 2n→∞. A fixed shift in the exponent does preserve Θ: Bn+c=BcBn, with Bc a constant. Parentheses matter: 2n2, (2n)2=22n, and 2n2 have different growth rates.

4.3 Factorials and variable exponents

For n≥2, n!=1·2·⋯·n≤nn. At least the last ⌈n/2⌉ factors are at least n/2, giving n!≥(n/2)⌈n/2⌉. Taking logarithms yields an upper bound ln(n!)≤n ln n and a lower bound ln(n!)≥⌈n/2⌉ln(n/2). For n≥4, ln(n/2)≥(ln n)/2, so ln(n!)≥(n/4)ln n. Hence ln(n!)∈Θ(n ln n). This elementary sandwich establishes the class without invoking Stirling's sharper formula.

For any fixed B>1, compare ln(n!/Bn)=ln(n!)−n ln B. The lower bound above tends to infinity, so Bn∈o(n!). Meanwhile n!/nn→0: the first ⌊n/2⌋ factors of n!/nn=∏j=1n(j/n) are at most 1/2, while the rest are at most 1, so the product is at most 2−⌊n/2⌋. Consequently, for fixed positive ε,k and fixed B>1, a useful chain is

1 ≪ log log n ≪ (log n)k ≪ nε ≪ Bn ≪ n! ≪ nn.

Here f≪g abbreviates f∈o(g), and the first relation assumes the logarithms are defined and grow. The chain is illustrative, not a total ordering of every displayed family for every choice of parameters: placing (log n)k after log log n requires fixed k>0; the relative positions of different polynomial powers or different exponential bases need their own comparison. A more granular and unambiguous example is shown below. Each symbol means that the preceding function is little-oh of the following one.

log log n ≪ log n ≪ n1/3 ≪ n ≪ n log n ≪ n2 ≪ 2n ≪ n! ≪ nn

For a nonconstant exponent, taking logarithms is often the safest method: nlog2 n=2(log2 n)2. Its logarithm grows like (ln n)2, faster than the logarithm of every fixed power nc but slower than the logarithm of 2n. Thus for every fixed c>0, nc∈o(nlog2 n) and nlog2 n∈o(2n). The notation 2Θ(n) denotes a family of exponential-order expressions, not an ordinary algebraic value whose Θ can be canceled from an exponent.

5. Algebraic rules and the traps in applying them

5.1 Sum, maximum, product, and transitivity

Suppose f1∈O(g1) and f2∈O(g2), with every function eventually nonnegative. Beyond the larger of the two thresholds, f1+f2≤c1g1+c2g2≤(c1+c2)max(g1,g2). Thus f1+f2∈O(max(g1,g2)). If both summands are nonnegative, max(f1,f2)≤f1+f2≤2max(f1,f2); their sum and maximum are Θ-equivalent. This is the valid “largest term wins” principle for positive costs. Cancellation in a difference is outside its hypotheses.

Multiplication follows from multiplying two nonnegative witness inequalities: f1f2≤c1c2g1g2, so the product is an O bound. If both original relations are Θ, multiply their lower and upper witnesses to get a Θ product. Transitivity also uses shared eventual thresholds: if f≤c1g eventually and g≤c2h eventually, then f≤c1c2h beyond their maximum threshold. Reflexivity f∈Θ(f) holds for an eventually nonnegative f, including the zero function. For fixed c>0, cf∈Θ(f).

These rules do not prove a lower bound for a sum from an upper bound on one summand. They also do not allow subtraction: n2+n and n2−n are each Θ of n2, but their difference is 2n. If f,g>0 eventually and f∈Θ(g), dividing the two-sided witnesses gives 1/f∈Θ(1/g). A mere f∈O(g) gives a reciprocal lower bound when f>0, not necessarily reciprocal Θ; for example 1∈O(n) but 1∉Θ(1/n) after reciprocation.

5.2 Composition, logarithms of costs, and nonmonotone functions

If f∈O(g) and h maps large inputs to values tending to infinity, then f(h(n))∈O(g(h(n))), assuming h(n) lies in the domain. The condition matters: if h(n)=1 forever, the eventual part of the original bound tells us nothing about the composed values. If f∈Θ(g), the same condition preserves Θ. An arbitrary outer function cannot be applied to both sides of an O relation: from f≤cg one cannot conclude 2f∈O(2g). Take f=2n, g=n; f∈Θ(g), but 22n∉O(2n). Even a monotone outer operation may amplify a constant factor into a changing one.

If positive f∈Θ(g) and both grow beyond 1, logarithms have an additive constant difference, since ln c1+ln g≤ln f≤ln c2+ln g. If ln g→∞, then ln f∼ln g. If g tends to 1, logarithmic comparison can break: f=2, g=1 are Θ-equivalent, yet ln f is positive and ln g=0. State positivity and growth before taking logarithms of a complexity bound.

5.3 Two or more independent size parameters

For functions of n,m, define a claim relative to an admissible domain D⊆ℕ². One precise joint-tail convention says f∈OD(g) if constants c,N,M>0 exist such that 0≤f(n,m)≤cg(n,m) for every (n,m)∈D with both n≥N and m≥M. An alternative one-size measure could use n+m→∞; it is a different convention and can include paths with one parameter fixed. Name the convention before comparing multivariate functions. If a graph has n vertices and m edges, restrictions such as 0≤m≤n(n−1)/2 for a simple undirected graph belong in D. It is invalid to replace m by n without an assumption that relates them.

On unconstrained positive integer pairs, n+m∉O(n): choose m=n2, making the ratio 1+n unbounded. On the restricted domain m≤3n, n+m≤4n, so n+m∈Θ(n) because it is also at least n. A one-variable hierarchy is not a substitute for checking every allowed growth path.

Teaching through formulas and conceptual decisions

Decide the relation before comparing growth

For eventually positive g, f∈O(g) means one constant upper bound on f/g beyond some threshold. f∈Ω(g) means an eventual positive lower bound; Θ requires both. Little-oh requires f/g→0, a strictly stronger conclusion than boundedness. A positive finite ratio limit proves Θ, but the absence of a limit does not refute Θ: a ratio oscillating between 1 and 3 is still bounded above and below.

Transform exponents and logarithms exactly

For fixed positive bases with logarithms defined, alogbn=nlogba. This is an exact identity obtained by taking natural logarithms. In contrast, alogb2n has exponent proportional to (lnn)2 and grows faster than every fixed polynomial. Constants inside an exponent are not multiplicative constants outside it: 22n/2n=2n is unbounded.

For fixed integer r, (nr)=Θ(nr) because the numerator is a product of r linear factors and r! is constant. If r grows with n, this reasoning fails. In particular, central binomial coefficients are exponential up to a polynomial factor; the fixed-index theorem must not be silently generalized.

Cancellation and several variables need their own analysis

Knowing f,g∈Θ(n2) does not determine f-g: cancellation can leave zero, a linear term or an oscillatory residual. For two independent parameters, a proposed O(n) bound on n+m fails on the path m=n2. Conversely, n+m∈Θ(max(n,m)) follows from the two inequalities max(n,m)≤n+m≤2max(n,m). Choose parameter paths to refute a uniform claim.

Detailed derivation tutorials

The following complete proofs and implementations support the new examination problems. They develop the reasoning needed to derive formulas; the separately labeled examination bank below tests calculation, concepts and distractor decisions.

Each problem states what must be decided and why each step is valid. “Inspired by” identifies a source's technique; the statement and solution are original. These are instructional worked problems, not a request that the student answer a test before completing the first reading.

Tutorial 1 — Exhibit both witnesses for a polynomial

Task. Establish a tight bound for F(n)=7n3−5n2+12n+9, with explicit constants.

Solution. For n≥1, upper-bound each positive term by its cubic counterpart and discard the negative term: F(n)≤(7+12+9)n3=28n3. For the lower bound, 7n3−5n2=n2(7n−5)≥2n3 because 7n−5≥2n for n≥1. The remaining terms are nonnegative. Thus 2n3≤F(n)≤28n3 for every n≥1. The witnesses c1=2,c2=28,n0=1 prove F∈Θ(n3). A leading-term limit also works, but this construction directly verifies the definition. Technique inspired by Stanford CS161's polynomial witnesses.

Tutorial 2 — Refute an overoptimistic upper bound

Task. Decide whether n3+4n∈O(n2 log2n).

Solution. The ratio is (n3+4n)/(n2log2n)=n/log2n+4/(n log2n) for n>1. The first term tends to infinity because log2n∈o(n), proved in §4.1; the second is nonnegative. Hence no fixed upper constant can work, so the membership is false. Directly, for any c choose n so large that n/log2n>c, then n3+4n>cn2log2n. This refutes the eventual universal quantifier, not merely a finite sample.

Tutorial 3 — Little-oh versus big-oh

Task. Classify F(n)=n(log2n)3 relative to G(n)=n5/4, and explain why a finite positive ratio would change the answer.

Solution. Cancel the positive n: F/G=(log2n)3/n1/4→0 by the logarithm-versus-power proof, with fixed k=3,ε=1/4. Therefore F∈o(G), hence also F∈O(G), but F∉Ω(G). If instead the ratio tended to a fixed positive number, the lower and upper witness constants would both exist and the correct relation would be Θ rather than little-oh.

Tutorial 4 — Fix a broken logarithm-base shortcut

Task. Compare F(n)=lognn2 with G(n)=log2n on n≥2.

Solution. By definition lognn2=2. Thus F/G=2/log2n→0, proving F∈o(G). The usual assertion that logarithm bases differ only by a constant applies only when those bases are fixed independently of n. Here the base is the variable input size. The exact value 2 also makes clear that F∈Θ(1).

Tutorial 5 — Exponent position changes everything

Task. Order 2n3, (2n)3, and 2n3 by strict asymptotic growth.

Solution. The middle expression is 23n=8n. A polynomial is little-oh of a fixed-base exponential, so 2n3∈o(8n). For the remaining pair, the ratio 8n/2n3=23n−n3→0 because n3−3n→∞. Thus 2n3 ≪ (2n)3 ≪ 2n3. Parentheses are essential: the first expression has a constant coefficient, the second has a linear exponent, and the third has a cubic exponent. Reasoning type informed by MIT 6.006's exponential-comparison exercises.

Tutorial 6 — A binomial coefficient with a fixed lower index

Task. For a fixed integer r≥1, find a tight class of C(n,r) as n→∞.

Solution. The exact product is C(n,r)=n(n−1)⋯(n−r+1)/r!. Since r is fixed, r! is a constant. Divide by nr: the ratio is (1/r!)∏j=0r−1(1−j/n)→1/r!>0, because the finite product has r factors, each tending to 1. Therefore C(n,r)∈Θ(nr), and more sharply C(n,r)∼nr/r!. If r=r(n) grows, this finite-fixed-product proof no longer applies. Reasoning type informed by MIT 6.006's fixed-index binomial comparison.

Tutorial 7 — Cancellation defeats a naive dominant-term rule

Task. Simplify and classify F(n)=(n3+4n2+1)−(n3−2n2+n).

Solution. Expand the subtraction before applying any growth rule: F(n)=6n2−n+1. The leading surviving coefficient is positive, so dividing by n2 gives 6−1/n+1/n2→6. Thus F∈Θ(n2), and indeed F∼6n2. Treating each parenthesis as Θ of n3 and subtracting Θ classes would lose the cancellation and produce an unjustified answer.

Tutorial 8 — A nonexistent limit with a valid tight bound

Task. Let F(n)=4n for even n and F(n)=9n for odd n. Classify it relative to n and decide whether it is asymptotically equivalent to 6n.

Solution. Every positive n satisfies 4n≤F(n)≤9n, so F∈Θ(n). The ratio F(n)/(6n) alternates between 2/3 and 3/2, so it does not tend to 1; F∼6n is false. Lack of a ratio limit did not defeat Θ because two global envelopes hold. Technique informed by CMU's oscillation example and Princeton's limit counterexample.

Tutorial 9 — Functions that are genuinely incomparable

Task. Define F(n)=n for even n and F(n)=n3 for odd n. Compare F with G(n)=n2.

Solution. On even sizes F/G=1/n→0, so no positive constant can lower-bound the ratio on all sufficiently large sizes; F∉Ω(G). On odd sizes F/G=n→∞, so no fixed constant can upper-bound it on all sufficiently large sizes; F∉O(G). Therefore F∉Θ(G) and neither function is uniformly no faster or no slower under these one-sided relations. This is different from Problem 8, where the oscillation stayed within fixed factors.

Tutorial 10 — Take factorial logarithms without overclaiming

Task. Classify H(n)=log2((3n)!) relative to n log2n, for integer n≥1.

Solution. Section 4.3 proved ln(k!)∈Θ(k ln k). Apply it with k=3n: ln((3n)!)∈Θ(3n ln(3n)). Since ln(3n)=ln n+ln3∈Θ(ln n) for n≥2, this is Θ of n ln n. Dividing by fixed ln2 changes only the constant, so H∈Θ(n log2n). This does not imply (3n)!∈Θ(n!); factorials themselves are much more sensitive to the argument.

Tutorial 11 — Show a factorial ratio is unbounded

Task. Decide whether (2n)!∈O(n!) and whether their logarithms have the same Θ class.

Solution. The ratio is (2n)!/n!=∏j=n+12nj≥(n+1)n→∞, so (2n)!∉O(n!) and hence cannot be Θ of n!. Yet ln((2n)!)∈Θ(2n ln(2n))=Θ(n ln n) and ln(n!)∈Θ(n ln n), so the two logarithms are Θ-equivalent. A logarithm compresses a multiplicative gap into an additive one; equal logarithmic Θ classes do not imply equal original Θ classes. Reasoning type informed by MIT 6.006's factorial comparison.

Tutorial 12 — Compare a variable exponent to both neighboring classes

Task. For each fixed c>0, compare nc, nlog2n, and 2n.

Solution. Take base-two logarithms of ratios, which preserves their order because log2 is strictly increasing. For the first ratio, log2(nlog2n/nc)=(log2n)2−c log2n→∞; hence nc∈o(nlog2n). For the second, log2(2n/nlog2n)=n−(log2n)2→∞ by the logarithm-versus-power theorem. Thus nlog2n∈o(2n). The middle expression is superpolynomial for every fixed degree but subexponential relative to base 2 in this precise comparison.

Tutorial 13 — Floors, ceilings, and fixed shifts

Task. Determine the class of F(n)=⌈n/3⌉+⌊√n⌋, and decide whether F∼n/3.

Solution. The elementary floor/ceiling inequalities give n/3≤⌈n/3⌉<n/3+1 and √n−1<⌊√n⌋≤√n. Therefore n/3≤F(n)<n/3+1+√n for positive integers. Dividing by n/3 gives 1≤F(n)/(n/3)<1+3/n+3/√n→1. The squeeze theorem proves the sharper statement F∼n/3, which implies F∈Θ(n). The square-root and rounding errors are genuinely lower order; no exact equality was assumed.

Tutorial 14 — A two-parameter path invalidates a one-parameter guess

Task. On unconstrained positive integer pairs, decide whether F(n,m)=n2+m belongs to O(n2). Re-evaluate on D={(n,m):1≤m≤n2}.

Solution. On the unconstrained domain choose the allowed path m=n3. Then F/n2=1+n→∞, refuting a universal fixed constant. On D, n2≤F≤2n2, so F∈ΘD(n2) with witnesses 1,2. The answer changes because the domain changes; a bound on one path cannot establish a multivariate bound over all paths. Reasoning type informed by Princeton's multiple-parameter slides.

Tutorial 15 — Exposing an invalid subtraction of Θ classes

Task. Decide whether the information A∈Θ(n2) and B∈Θ(n2) determines the class of A−B.

Solution. It does not. Three examples, all with nonnegative A,B, show why. If A=n2 and B=n2, their difference is identically zero. If A=n2+n and B=n2, the difference is n∈Θ(n). If A=2n2 and B=n2, the difference is n2∈Θ(n2). All three satisfy the same two premises. One must analyze the actual expressions or establish additional information, such as their leading coefficients or a bound on the difference.

Tutorial 16 — An algorithm's upper bound and a problem's lower bound

Task. A problem has a proved worst-case lower bound Ω(n log n) for every algorithm in a stated comparison model. Algorithm A has a proved worst-case upper bound O(n log n) in the same model. What follows? What if its upper bound were only O(n2)?

Solution. The universal problem lower bound applies to A in that model. Combined with its upper bound, TA,worst∈Θ(n log n), and no algorithm in that model can have an asymptotically smaller worst-case order than this lower bound. If the only upper bound on A is O(n2), then we know TA,worst∈Ω(n log n)∩O(n2), but no Θ class follows: n log n, n3/2, and n2 all fit those one-sided constraints. A lower bound on one algorithm alone would not establish a problem lower bound. Reasoning type informed by CMU's asymptotic optimality discussion.

Tutorial 17 — Composition and exponentiation are different moves

Task. Given f(t)=2t and g(t)=t, let h(n)=⌊√n⌋. Compare f∘h with g∘h, then compare 2f(n) with 2g(n).

Solution. Because f(t)=2g(t) for every t, substitution gives f(h(n))=2g(h(n)); hence they are Θ-equivalent. The fact that h(n)→∞ also satisfies the general composition condition. Exponentiating the values is a different operation: 2f(n)/2g(n)=2n→∞. Therefore 2f(n)∉O(2g(n)). A fixed multiplicative difference in exponents is not a fixed multiplicative difference in exponentials.

Tutorial 18 — Tightness, equivalence, and a finite crossover

Task. Compare P(n)=400n+20 and Q(n)=n2+20 both asymptotically and at n=100. Determine whether P∼400n.

Solution. P(n)/n=400+20/n→400, so P∈Θ(n); Q(n)/n2=1+20/n2→1, so Q∈Θ(n2). Thus P/Q→0 and P∈o(Q). At n=100, however, P(100)=40020 while Q(100)=10020; the quadratic expression is smaller there. Their difference is P−Q=400n−n2=n(400−n), so the positive-size crossover is n=400. Finally, P/(400n)=1+1/(20n)→1, so P∼400n. The fixed numbers describe these symbolic functions only; no hardware performance follows without measuring implementations.

Authentic examination questions

Question 1. PhD CE 1405, Q1 — Unequal recursive splits

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 2 · question 1. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Fixed positive constants α,β satisfy α+β=1. For

T(n)=T(αn)+T(βn)+n

with constant small-input base cost, which listed bound is correct?

1.
O(αβn)
2.
O(nlogn)
3.
O(βnαlogn)
4.
O(αn+βlogn)
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

  1. The Akra–Bazzi exponent satisfies αp+βp=1. Here p=1.
  2. Its integral is ∫1nu/u2du=logn, giving T(n)=Θ(nlogn). Integer rounding of subproblem sizes is absorbed under the usual bounded-perturbation convention.
  3. Constants α,β are fixed; options 1 and 4 are linear bounds and are too small. Since 0<α<1, option 3 grows as nαlogn=o(nlogn) and is also too small.
  4. The equal-split Master theorem does not directly apply to unequal branches; equal sizes cannot be invented.

Transfer rule. Solve for the branching exponent before comparing candidate bounds; coefficients and exponents play different roles.

Concept model supporting this solution

This is a separate teaching example of Critical recurrence: equal work at each level. Its numeric values are not the data or answer of this question. Use the stated invariant to interpret the written solution.

Question 2. PhD CE 1405, Q2 — A polylogarithmic toll

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 2 · question 2. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

What is the order of

T(n)=T(2n/3)+log2n

, with bounded base cost?

1.
Θ(n)
2.
Θ(log2n)
3.
Θ(log3n)
4.
Θ(logn)
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

  1. There is one recursive branch and Θ(logn) levels. At level j, the toll is (logn-jlog(3/2))2 until the argument reaches the base region.
  2. The upper bound is O(logn) tolls each at most O(log2n), giving O(log3n).
  3. In the first fixed fraction of the levels, each logarithm remains Θ(logn), so there are Θ(logn) tolls of size Θ(log2n). This gives the matching lower bound.
  4. Option 2 counts only the root toll; option 4 counts only levels; option 1 is a loose upper bound but the question asks the tight order.

Transfer rule. A tight estimate needs both the number of significant levels and their accumulated toll.

Concept model supporting this solution

This is a separate teaching example of Critical recurrence: equal work at each level. Its numeric values are not the data or answer of this question. Use the stated invariant to interpret the written solution.

Question 3. MSc CE 1405, Q58 — A square-root recurrence

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 13 · question 58. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

Which listed bound describes T(n)=2T(⌊n⌋)+logn with bounded base cost?

1.
O(lognloglogn)
2.
O(nloglogn)
3.
O(loglogn)
4.
O(logn)
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

  1. Let m=log2n and first ignore the harmless floor to see the structure. The recurrence becomes S(m)=2S(m/2)+m.
  2. Each of its Θ(logm) significant levels costs Θ(m), so S(m)=Θ(mlogm).
  3. Substitute back to obtain Θ(lognloglogn). A base region above one prevents the square-root recursion from sticking at one.
  4. Option 2 is also a loose upper bound. As is conventional in this source question, option 1 is the smallest asymptotic bound among the listed choices. Options 3 and 4 are too small. The booklet uses O rather than Θ, so the literal wording does not make all true upper bounds mutually exclusive.

Source wording note. The tight answer is unambiguous; selecting a unique O answer requires the usual smallest-bound convention.

Concept model supporting this solution

This is a separate teaching example of Critical recurrence: equal work at each level. Its numeric values are not the data or answer of this question. Use the stated invariant to interpret the written solution.

Question 4. PhD CS 1404, Q71 — A multiplicative one-step recurrence

Authentic examination · English translation

Original booklet · PDF page 16 · question 71. independently derived; not represented as an official key.

For T(n)=2nT(n-1) and T(0)=1, which listed order is correct?

1.
Θ(n2n)
2.
Θ(2nlogn)
3.
Θ(2n2)
4.
Θ((2)n2+n)
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 4.

  1. Unroll the recurrence:
T(n)=∏j=1n2j=2∑j=1nj=2n(n+1)/2

. 2. The last option is exactly (2)n2+n=2(n2+n)/2. 3. Option 3 is not a tight bound: its ratio to the true answer is 2(n2-n)/2 and grows without bound. Option 2 is far smaller. The exponent of option 1 is 2nlog2n, also much smaller than n(n+1)/2 eventually. 4. Constants multiplying an exponent of n2 cannot be discarded inside a tight exponential order.

Transfer rule. Take logarithms or add exponents when recurrence terms multiply.

Question 5. Two true upper bounds but one tight class

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CE_1405_Q58; Phd_CE_1405_Q1. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Let f(n)=nlogn+n3/4. Which conjunction is correct?

1.

f∈Θ(n) and f∈O(nlogn)

2.

f∈Θ(nlogn) and f∈O(n2)

3.

f∈o(nlogn) and f∈O(n2)

4.

f∈Θ(n2) and f∈O(nlogn)

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

Divide by nlogn: the ratio is 1+n-1/4/logn, tending to one. Thus the tight order is nlogn.

That function is also bounded above by a constant times n2 eventually. A larger upper bound can be true without being tight; the first and third alternatives misclassify the leading term, and the fourth asserts mutually incompatible tight orders.

Question 6. A factor inside an exponential cannot be suppressed

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1404_Q71. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Which statement is correct for f(n)=2n2+n and g(n)=2n2?

1.
f∈Θ(g)
2.
f∈o(g)
3.
g∈o(f)
4.
f/g=n
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

Their ratio is f/g=2n, which diverges. Therefore g/f=2-n tends to zero, so g∈o(f).

An additive linear term in a quadratic exponent multiplies the final value by an unbounded exponential factor. It cannot be removed inside a tight bound. The final alternative treats exponentiation as if it were addition outside the exponential.

Question 7. Oscillation defeats a tight bound

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q2; MS_CE_1405_Q58. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

f(n)=n for even n and n2 for odd n. Which classification is correct?

1.
f∈Θ(n)
2.
f∈Θ(n2)
3.

f∈O(n2)∩Ω(n) but neither listed tight class

4.
f∉O(n2)
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

For every positive n, n≤f(n)≤n2, so both one-sided bounds hold. Along odd inputs, f(n)/n=n is unbounded, excluding O(n) and hence Θ(n).

Along even inputs, f(n)/n2=1/n tends to zero, excluding Ω(n2) and hence Θ(n2). Bounds must hold uniformly after a threshold, not just on a favorable subsequence.

Question 8. Cancellation before classifying a function

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: MS_CE_1405_Q58; Phd_CE_1405_Q2. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

For positive integers n, simplify the growth of f(n)=n2+n-n.

1.
Θ(n)
2.
Θ(n)
3.
Θ(1)
4.
Θ(1/n)
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

Rationalize:

f(n)=n/(n2+n+n)=1/(1+1/n+1)

. It tends to one half and is positive, so its tight order is constant.

Classifying the two large terms separately would miss their cancellation. The denominator and numerator after rationalization both have linear scale. A nonzero finite limiting value gives upper and lower positive constant bounds eventually.

Question 11. The floor in an exponent

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q2; MS_CE_1405_Q58. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Compare f(n)=2⌊log2n⌋ to n. Which bounds hold for all positive n?

1.
n/2<f(n)≤n
2.
n≤f(n)<2n
3.
f(n)=n
4.
f(n)≤log2n
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 1.

Let k=⌊log2n⌋. Then 2k≤n<2k+1. Rearranging the strict upper inequality gives n/2<2k.

Thus the first bounds hold and imply Θ(n). Equality holds only at powers of two; the floor introduces an oscillating ratio between just above one half and one, not a change in the tight class. Testing n=3 eliminates the equality and reversed-bound choices.

Question 12. A factorial comparison using logarithms

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CS_1404_Q71; MS_CS_1405_Q120. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Which statement is correct as n grows?

1.
n!∈O(2n)
2.
2n∈o(n!)
3.
n!∈Θ(nn)
4.
log(n!)∈Θ(n)
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 2.

The final half of the factorial's factors are each at least n/2. Thus n!≥(n/2)n/2, whose ratio to 2n eventually diverges; hence 2n=o(n!).

Stirling or elementary log-sum bounds give log(n!)=Θ(nlogn), ruling out the last option. Also n!/nn tends to zero, since at least half the factors are at most n/2, giving a factor at most 2-n/2. Upper bounds alone do not establish a tight class.

Question 13. An exact ratio before taking a limit — exact instance 1

Original examination analogue · author-assessed medium difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q1; Phd_CE_1405_Q2. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

For F(n)=3n2+5n, calculate F(n)/n2. Calculate the requested quantity for n=5.

1.
8
2.
28
3.
4
4.
3
Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 3.

Step 1 — model and conditions. Divide every term by the same normalizing power. The lower-degree term becomes 5/n, which tends to zero but remains present in every exact finite ratio. The limiting constant supports a tight quadratic bound because it is positive and finite.

Step 2 — compute. The general expression is 3+5/n. Substituting n=5 gives 4. Keep the exact value until all constraints have been applied.

Step 3 — audit the alternatives. The other listed values are 3, 8, 28. They are obtained from the three competing expressions 3, 8, 3+5n, respectively. Those expressions discard or alter a condition in the model; the derivation above shows where the discrepancy enters. Recomputing the defining constraints, rather than selecting the numerically nearest option, determines the answer.

Question 16. An exact ratio before taking a limit — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q1; Phd_CE_1405_Q2. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

For F(n)=3n2+5n, calculate F(n)/n2. Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method?

1.

Lower-order terms are zero at every finite size.

2.

A positive finite ratio limit gives only an upper bound.

3.

A zero ratio limit proves the numerator is identically zero.

4.

A limiting ratio is not necessarily the exact finite ratio.

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 4.

Check the hypothesis. Limits describe eventual behavior. A positive finite limit gives both upper and lower constant bounds for all sufficiently large sizes. A zero limit gives little-o behavior, while exact arithmetic still retains any nonzero lower-order terms.

Connect it to the calculation. Divide every term by the same normalizing power. The lower-degree term becomes 5/n, which tends to zero but remains present in every exact finite ratio. The limiting constant supports a tight quadratic bound because it is positive and finite. The valid statement is: A limiting ratio is not necessarily the exact finite ratio. A formula can remain numerically correct in one exceptional case after its assumptions are removed, but that does not justify using it as a general rule. Distinguish the mathematical identity from the modeling assumptions that permit this identity to count or measure the requested objects.

Step 1 — model and conditions. The defining inequality gives a ceiling logarithm. For exact evaluation compare neighboring integer powers with the factorial. For growth, at least half the factorial factors are at least n/2, while every factor is at most n, giving tight order nlogn.

Step 2 — compute. The general expression is ⌈log2(n!)⌉. Substituting n=5 gives 7. Keep the exact value until all constraints have been applied.

Step 3 — audit the alternatives. The other listed values are 6, 25, 15. They are obtained from the three competing expressions ⌊log2(n!)⌋, n2, n⌈log2n⌉, respectively. Those expressions discard or alter a condition in the model; the derivation above shows where the discrepancy enters. Recomputing the defining constraints, rather than selecting the numerically nearest option, determines the answer.

Question 44. A factorial leaf count and its integer logarithm — applicability and boundary

Original examination analogue · author-assessed hard difficulty

Pattern reference: Phd_CE_1405_Q1; Phd_CE_1405_Q2. This is an original problem, not a question from those booklets.

Find the smallest integer h such that 2h≥n!. Which statement correctly identifies the scope or a failure of this method?

1.

Taking a logarithm preserves every growth order.

2.

The floor always meets a greater-than-or-equal power threshold.

3.

Factorial growth is polynomial because its logarithm has polynomial size.

4.

A bound on the logarithm of a factorial is not a bound on the factorial itself.

Read the complete solution and option analysis

Correct option: 4.

Check the hypothesis. Logarithms compress products into sums and can radically change growth classes. The ceiling is required by the integer threshold. A polynomial-size representation or logarithm of a quantity does not imply that enumerating that many objects takes polynomial time.

Connect it to the calculation. The defining inequality gives a ceiling logarithm. For exact evaluation compare neighboring integer powers with the factorial. For growth, at least half the factorial factors are at least n/2, while every factor is at most n, giving tight order nlogn. The valid statement is: A bound on the logarithm of a factorial is not a bound on the factorial itself. A formula can remain numerically correct in one exceptional case after its assumptions are removed, but that does not justify using it as a general rule. Distinguish the mathematical identity from the modeling assumptions that permit this identity to count or measure the requested objects.

Integrated multistep challenges

Question 45. Oscillation across growth classes

Original integrated challenge · retained after review

For positive integer n, let f(n)=n2+sin(lnn) and g(n)=n2. Which statement holds?

1. f∈Θ(g)

2. f∈O(g) but not Ω(g)

3. f∈Ω(g) but not O(g)

4. Neither big-oh nor big-omega relation holds.

Correct option: 4.

The ratio is nsin(lnn). Near logarithmic phases π/2+2kπ, it grows like n and is unbounded. Near 3π/2+2kπ, it behaves like 1/n and tends to zero. Integer indices can be chosen by rounding the corresponding exponentials; their logarithmic error tends to zero. Thus no uniform upper constant or positive lower constant works. A ratio lacking a limit does not always cause incomparability, but these two subsequences do.

Question 46. A floor inside an exponent

Original integrated challenge · retained after review

For n≥1, what is the relation between f(n)=2⌊log2n⌋ and n?

1. f∈Θ(n), but f/n need not converge.

2. f∈o(n)

3. f∈ω(n)

4. f/n→1

Correct option: 1.

If 2k≤n<2k+1, then f=2k, so n/2<f≤n. These constant bounds establish tight linear growth. At powers of two the ratio is1, while near the top of each interval it tends to1/2. Hence there is no limit1 or any single ratio limit. Rounding the logarithm changes a bounded factor without creating a strict growth relation.

Applicable formulas and examination notes

1. Ratio outcomes

For eventually positive g, a ratio limit 0 gives little-oh; a positive finite limit gives tight order; infinity gives little-omega. Failure of a limit leaves the question open: bounded positive oscillation can still give tight order.

2. Polynomial versus logarithm

For fixed ε>0, (logn)k/nε→0 for fixed k. Thus nlogn∈o(n1.1). A varying exponent or logarithm power is not covered by the fixed-parameter theorem.

3. Move exponents correctly

alogbn=nlogba for fixed valid bases. Thus 4log2n=n2. Squaring the logarithm in the exponent instead yields superpolynomial growth; parentheses determine which expression is being compared.

4. Exponential ratios

Compare acn with an by the ratio a(c-1)n for fixed a>1. When c>1, the ratio diverges. A coefficient inside an exponent is not a dispensable outside constant.

5. Factorial logarithms

Use log(n!)=∑j=1nlogj and upper/lower blocks to establish Θ(nlogn). This does not imply n!∈Θ(nn): exponentiating a tight-order logarithm does not preserve multiplicative tight order.

6. Fixed binomial index

(nr)∈Θ(nr) only when r is a fixed nonnegative integer. For r=4, expand four linear factors and divide by24. If r grows with n, analyze its factorials instead of treating r! as constant.

7. Subtract actual functions

Expand (n+1)3-n3 before selecting its dominant term; the answer is quadratic. Bounds on each operand alone do not specify the difference. A difference can even be zero or change sign.

8. Independent variables

n+m∈Θ(max(n,m)) uniformly, with constants 1 and 2. To reject a single-variable guess, choose a legal path such as m=n2. A relation imposed between parameters can change the answer and must be stated.

9. Quantified bound witnesses

To prove big-oh, give a constant c and threshold n0 working for every larger input. To refute it, show that every proposed c,n0 admits a violating larger input. A few measured values establish neither statement.

10. Hierarchy through log differences

For nlog2n, compare lnf with the log of a candidate using their difference, not just their ratio. The difference with a fixed polynomial log diverges upward; the difference with nln2 diverges downward. This gives strict ratio conclusions.

11. Little relations and transitivity

f∈o(g) implies f∈O(g) but not conversely. f∈Θ(g) is symmetric, while big-oh is not. With positive functions, transitivity preserves upper bounds; subtracting or exponentiating their class labels generally does not preserve a tight relation.

12. Floors and shifts

For fixed positive c, ⌊cn⌋ is tightly linear once n is large. A fixed additive shift does not alter a monotone polynomial's order, but applying it inside an arbitrary oscillating or exponential-indexed function requires analysis of that actual function.

13. Upper algorithm versus lower problem bound

An algorithm's upper bound establishes existence of one method with that cost. A problem lower bound quantifies over every algorithm in the specified model. A slow algorithm cannot prove a problem requires its runtime.
